name: Reading Central Bank Communication
title: Reading Central Bank Communication
answer: Reading central bank communication is the systematic study of what monetary policy makers say and write, from rate decisions and statements to minutes, speeches, interviews and press conferences. In macroeconomic econometrics it turns that language into variables that can be used in models of inflation, output, interest rates and expectations. The work covers both the content of the message, such as the policy stance and forward guidance, and its tone, uncertainty and emphasis. It also covers how those signals differ across central banks and over time. This topic sits within The AI Economist, where text analysis meets macro modelling.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Reading central bank communication is the systematic study of what monetary policy makers say and write, from rate decisions and statements to minutes, speeches, interviews and press conferences. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on document collections gathered from central bank websites, official archives and press offices, together with metadata such as speaker, date and meeting. Processing typically uses Python or R, natural language processing libraries, and increasingly large language models for summarisation, classification and question answering. Storage and compute range from a laptop for small studies to cloud clusters and GPUs for large transformer models. Version control and databases keep track of documents, annotations and model outputs. Human coders remain part of the pipeline for validation and for cases where judgement matters.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common approach starts with a clear question, such as whether a statement shifted the expected path of policy, then builds a corpus and a coding scheme. Dictionary methods count words from predefined lists, supervised models learn from human labelled examples, and topic models or embeddings find recurring themes without labels. Transformer based models and prompted large language models can classify sentences, extract forward guidance and summarise paragraphs, but their outputs need checking against human reading. The resulting text measures are then used in regressions, event studies, vector autoregressions or local projections to relate communication to asset prices, forecasts or macroeconomic outcomes. Careful work separates the signal from the noise and tests whether results hold across speakers, meetings and policy regimes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Central bank documents are usually public, but their reuse can still be governed by copyright, terms of use and attribution requirements, and some research relies on licensed or paywalled sources. Provenance matters, so each text should carry its source, date, speaker, meeting and version, because a later revision can change the meaning. Risks include look ahead bias when a model uses information that was not available at the time, overfitting to one policy era, and spurious correlations between words and market moves. Large language models add risks of hallucination, unstable outputs and opaque training data, so documentation and reproducibility are essential. Governance usually means clear data handling rules, audit trails, human review and disclosure of model limitations.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real time analysis of speeches and press conferences, including voice and video, rather than only archived text. Multilingual and cross country comparisons are becoming more common as researchers seek common measures of policy tone and uncertainty. Large language models are likely to handle more of the extraction and summarisation, with human economists focusing on validation and interpretation. Central banks themselves are also using text analysis to monitor their own communication and public expectations. The open questions are how to measure uncertainty reliably, how to compare signals across regimes, and how to keep models transparent enough for policy work.
